>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst.
After meeting with the Prime Minister of Qatar
in Washington today, President Trump held an impromptu press
conference from the White House saying he's standing
by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, even in the face
of an impeachment effort filed today
by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massey.
A vote is expected this week.
>> Yeah, I'll stand by it.
>> So even if he's impeached, you're going to keep him.
>> I'll stand by it.
>> You're Defense Secretary.
>> He went to wars.
He was in charge.
We all won.
>> Trump was apparently speaking about Iran and Venezuela,
which was the object of a military operation
to seize its president, to stand trial in New York
and claim its oil, but didn't wage a war.
Trump also defended the US war in Iran.
Before the massive Republican losses in the midterm elections,
Trump had said he may attack Iran again after,
but today says he thinks the war is militarily over,
though he says the US remains ready should that change.
The French government is alleging
that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was
behind last month's cyber attack that hacked hundreds
of supermarket refrigeration systems across the country,
costing millions in spoiled food.
Iran has yet to respond to the accusations,
as Rebecca Rossman reports from Paris.
>> The French foreign minister called the attack, quote,
"unprecedented" and suggested Iran would face more EU sanctions.
The Paris prosecutor's office, meanwhile,
says it has opened an investigation
into a cyber unit linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
It began in October with a cyber attack
on some 700 commercial fridges and freezers across France,
sending temperatures soaring to over 120 degrees Fahrenheit.
Some fridges even caught fire.
Supermarkets were forced to throw away millions of dollars
worth of spoiled food.
Last week, other countries in Europe
were hit with similar attacks.
It's unclear if the incidents are linked.
Rebecca Rossman, NPR News, Paris.
>> The Food and Drug Administration
is requiring drug makers to add a new warning
to the labels of popular GLP-1 drugs.
And, here, Sydney Lupkin reports,
it's about a rare eye condition
that can lead to permanent vision loss.
>> The FDA says there's potentially an increased risk
of a rare eye problem associated with GLP-1 medications.
It's called non-arteritic anterior ischemic
optic neuropathy, or NION.
And it's caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve.
The condition is usually painless
and results in vision loss in one eye that can be permanent.
The FDA is requiring drug companies making GLP-1s
to add information about NION
to the warning sections of their labels.
GLP-1 drugs include Ozimpic and Wagovi,
as well as Manjaro, Zepbond, and Foundeo.
They also include drugs like Trulicity and Victoza.
Patients should be aware of the risk
and contact their doctors right away
if they experience vision symptoms while taking these drugs.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
>> You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
>> Reducing air pollution
to World Health Organization guidelines
could save 9 million lives a year,
according to new research.
As NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports,
the vast majority of people live under skies
that exceed those guidelines.
>> Air pollution spewed by power plants, factories, or cars
is seriously bad for health.
Studies show it can raise risk of ailments
as diverse as heart disease and dementia.
In light of that research, the WHO issued tighter guidelines
on air pollution in 2021.
A new study in the journal Environment International
estimates meeting those guidelines
could have big benefits for low- and middle-income countries.
They found that 9.4 million deaths,
mostly due to heart disease and stroke,
could be averted each year under the guidelines.
In addition, cutting air pollution
could prevent millions of new cases of these diseases
from ever developing.
Those potential benefits are far off for many, however,
as the WHO estimates that over 90% of the global population
lives in places that don't meet current guidelines.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
>> A fraternity at Ohio State University
has been temporarily suspended
while authorities investigate a video
that appears to show two people with their clothing in flames.
A university spokesperson says the Sigma Alpha Epsilon
fraternity is on interim suspension
while the school investigates
and says that those involved are getting medical treatment.
It's been referred to police who say
it appears the event took place on Saturday.
The fraternity says it is cooperating with the investigation
and that it will take appropriate action.
U.S. futures contracts are trading slightly higher.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
